records.question: What is asthma?
records.answer: Asthma is a common condition that affects the airways in and out of your lungs. These airways can become sensitive and inflamed, making it harder to breathe and causing symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. (section: what-is-asthma)

records.question: Which inhaler do I need to take every day?
records.answer: The preventer inhaler needs to be taken every day, even if you are symptom free. (section: treatment)

records.question: My mouth gets sore after using my inhaler. What can I do about it?
records.answer: Rinsing your mouth after using your inhaler can reduce the chance of it becoming sore. (section: treatment)

records.question: What are the common triggers for asthma symptoms?
records.answer: Common triggers for asthma symptoms include: colds and viruses, allergies (e.g., animal hair, pollen), dust, pollution, smoke, stress or heightened emotions, temperature extremes or changes, hormones, strong smells (e.g., perfumes, aerosols, cleaning products), and exercise (in some cases). (section: triggers)

records.question: How is asthma diagnosed?
records.answer: Asthma is diagnosed based on your symptom history and the results of breathing tests. (section: how-diagnosed)

records.question: Can exercise bring on my asthma symptoms?
records.answer: Yes, exercise can bring on asthma symptoms, which is known as exercise-induced asthma. Using a reliever medication before exercise can often prevent symptoms. (section: triggers)

records.question: Where can I find more reliable information about asthma?
records.answer: Asthma and Lung UK website is an excellent source of useful, reliable, and up to date information. (section: further-info)

records.question: How do I get this leaflet in Braille or large print?
records.answer: To get this leaflet in Braille or large print, contact the Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS): • 01752 439694 • Plh-tr.PALS@nhs.net (section: further-info)

records.question: What is the maximum number of puffs of my reliever inhaler during an asthma attack?
records.answer: The maximum number of puffs of your reliever inhaler during an asthma attack is 10 puffs. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: During an attack, how often should I take a puff?
records.answer: Every 30-60 seconds, up to a maximum of 10 puffs. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: How many times a week can I use my reliever and still count as well controlled?
records.answer: You can use your reliever inhaler up to 3 times per week and still count as well controlled. (section: well-controlled)

records.question: What proportion of people with asthma have severe asthma?
records.answer: Around 5% of all people with asthma have a diagnosis of severe asthma. (section: is-it-serious)

records.question: While waiting for the ambulance, how long should I wait before repeating the puffs?
records.answer: While waiting for the ambulance, you should repeat step 2 (taking one puff of your reliever inhaler every 30-60 seconds up to a maximum of 10 puffs) after 15 minutes. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: I keep waking up at night with a tight chest. Does that mean my treatment is working?
records.answer: No, waking up at night with a tight chest is a sign that your asthma may not be well controlled. (section: well-controlled)

records.question: Does this run in families?
records.answer: Yes, asthma can run in families. (section: why-people-get-asthma)

records.question: Will I ever be completely free of this?
records.answer: Asthma is a generally a lifelong condition, and there is no cure. However, with proper treatment, most people can be symptom free most of the time. (section: treatment)

records.question: I feel completely fine at the moment. Can I stop taking my steroid inhaler?
records.answer: The documents do not provide specific guidance on stopping a steroid inhaler if you feel fine. It is important to consult your healthcare provider before making any changes to your medication. (section: treatment)

records.question: I've been getting a tight chest and a whistling sound when I breathe at night. Is that asthma?
records.answer: The symptoms you describe—tight chest and a whistling sound when breathing at night—could be related to asthma, as these are common symptoms of asthma attacks. However, only a healthcare professional can diagnose asthma. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: My son was born six weeks early. Does that make asthma more likely for him?
records.answer: Yes, premature birth is thought to be a risk factor for asthma. (section: why-people-get-asthma)

records.question: My job is really dusty and I've started wheezing. Could the two be connected?
records.answer: The connection between a dusty work environment and wheezing could be relevant, as occupational exposure to certain substances such as dust can lead to asthma in some individuals. However, the documents do not provide a direct link between your specific situation and wheezing. (section: why-people-get-asthma)

records.question: I'm going through the menopause and I've suddenly become breathless. Is that related?
records.answer: The documents mention that hormonal changes, including those during menopause, can play a part in asthma. However, sudden breathlessness could be a symptom of an asthma attack or another condition. For accurate assessment and advice, consult a healthcare professional. (section: why-people-get-asthma)

records.question: I use my reliever about five times a week and I had an attack last month. What should I do?
records.answer: Your asthma is not well controlled. You should consult your healthcare provider to review your treatment plan and manage your symptoms effectively. (section: well-controlled, section: treatment)

records.question: List, in order, everything I should do the moment an asthma attack starts.
records.answer: Sit up straight – don’t lie down. Try to keep calm. Take one puff of your reliever inhaler every 30-60 seconds up to a maximum of 10 puffs. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: Why might someone only develop asthma as an adult rather than as a child?
records.answer: Occupational exposure to certain substances such as dust or chemicals can lead to asthma in some individuals. Hormones can play a part – after puberty more girls than boys get asthma, and some women develop late-onset asthma during or after the menopause. Smoking, secondary exposure to smoke, and air pollution are also thought to be risk factors. (section: why-people-get-asthma)

records.question: How much does an inhaler cost?
records.answer: The information is not in the available documents. (section: treatment, asthma-attack, further-info)

records.question: Can I take ibuprofen together with my asthma medication?
records.answer: The available documents do not provide information on taking ibuprofen together with asthma medication. Consult your healthcare provider for advice on drug interactions. (section: treatment, is-it-serious)

records.question: Which doctors at your hospital specialise in asthma?
records.answer: The information is not in the available documents. (section: further-info, treatment, is-it-serious)

records.question: What dose of prednisolone should I take for an asthma flare-up?
records.answer: The available documents do not provide information on the dose of prednisolone for an asthma flare-up. (section: treatment, well-controlled, asthma-attack)

records.question: I'm having an asthma attack right now. What do I do?
records.answer: Sit up straight and try to keep calm. Take one puff of your reliever inhaler every 30-60 seconds up to a maximum of 10 puffs. If you feel worse or don’t feel better after 10 puffs, call 999 for an ambulance. Repeat step 2 after 15 minutes while waiting for an ambulance. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: I've taken 10 puffs and I don't feel better. Can I just take 5 more?
records.answer: No, if you have taken 10 puffs of your reliever inhaler and still do not feel better, you should call 999 for an ambulance immediately. Do not take additional puffs. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: Hen suyễn là bệnh gì?
records.answer: Hen suyễn là một tình trạng y tế liên quan đến đường hô hấp, trong đó các đường thở bị viêm và sưng, gây ra các triệu chứng như ho, thở khò khè, cảm giác tức ngực và khó thở. Thông tin chi tiết về hen suyễn có thể được tìm thấy tại trang web của Asthma and Lung UK: https://www.asthma.org.uk/ (section: further-info)

records.question: Lên cơn hen thì được xịt tối đa bao nhiêu nhát?
records.answer: Tối đa 10 nhát. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: Thuốc xịt cắt cơn khác thuốc xịt dự phòng như thế nào?
records.answer: Thông tin trong các tài liệu không cung cấp sự khác biệt giữa thuốc xịt cắt cơn và thuốc xịt dự phòng. (section: further-info, well-controlled, asthma-attack)

records.question: Những yếu tố nào có thể khởi phát cơn hen?
records.answer: Thông tin trong tài liệu không đề cập đến các yếu tố có thể khởi phát cơn hen. (section: further-info, well-controlled, asthma-attack)
